title: The Nightmare
source: Detroit Institute of Arts (public domain: Fuseli died in 1825). Wikimedia Commons: Johann Heinrich Füssli - The Nightmare 55.5.A-d1-2019-04-15.jpg, 8192x6577, saved at 8000 px.
caption: Have you ever woken up and couldn't move? This painting is about that. #art #arthistory #painting #oilpainting #museum
_verify: VERIFIED 2026-10-11 (Wikipedia 'The Nightmare'): 1781, Detroit Institute of Arts; first shown 1782 at the Royal Academy, shocked critics, first commercial success; sleeping woman draped over the bed, head hanging down; incubus peers out at the viewer; horse head through the curtains with pupil-less eyes; early meaning of nightmare = weight on the chest + sleep paralysis; back of the canvas: unfinished portrait of a girl that may be Anna Landolt, Fuseli's unrequited love; H.W. Janson suggested the demon is Fuseli himself; Thomas Burke engraving from 1783 earned the publisher 500+ pounds; Frankenstein (1818) scene likely drew from it.
'Mare' = a spirit/goblin that sits on sleepers (Old English mære): standard etymology, not from the page above.
Freud print: only Max Eastman's 1926 account; not used.

slides.headline: Have you ever woken up and couldn't move?
London, 1782
slides.text: The Royal Academy opens its doors. And visitors stop in front of this painting, shocked.

slides.headline: A woman asleep
slides.text: She lies across the bed, head hanging down, arms thrown back. Deep asleep. Or is she?

slides.headline: But she's not alone
slides.text: A demon crouches on her chest, staring straight at you.

slides.headline: And then, through the curtain
slides.text: A horse's head pushes in, with blank eyes and no pupils.

slides.headline: It's not about the horse
slides.text: The 'mare' in nightmare was a spirit that sat on sleepers' chests. Today we call it sleep paralysis.

slides.headline: Is the demon the painter?
slides.text: One art historian thought so. Fuseli loved a young woman, Anna Landolt. She never loved him back.

slides.headline: And on the back of the canvas
slides.text: Turn it around and there is an unfinished portrait of a girl. It may be Anna.

slides.headline: It haunted everyone
slides.text: Prints spread across Europe. Decades later, Mary Shelley wrote a scene in Frankenstein that looks just like it.
